aspects.says: A ConcurrentHashMap iterator is weakly consistent: it never throws ConcurrentModificationException, returns each element at most once, and may or may not reflect changes made after it was created.
basis: section:6.5.3.3. Concurrent Collections and Their Iteration Guarantees

aspects.says: A CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator throws UnsupportedOperationException from remove(); the list's own remove or removeIf is used instead.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator walks the array the list had when the iterator was created, so it neither sees later adds and removes nor throws.
basis: section:6.5.3.3. Concurrent Collections and Their Iteration Guarantees

aspects.says: Fail-fast detection is best-effort, may miss a change made by another thread, and must never drive program logic.
basis: section:6.5.3.1. Iteration and Modification in Non-Concurrent Collections
aspects.reason: a claim that detection can fail across threads, which no deterministic test can show; the tracked practice builds the single-threaded detection it qualifies

aspects.says: List.of, Set.of and Map.of collections cannot change structurally, so their iterators never throw ConcurrentModificationException.
aspects.reason: a direct consequence of immutability with nothing further to practise

aspects.says: The iterator's own remove() is safe during iteration because it updates the iterator's expected count along with the list's.
While walking a HashMap, entry.setValue is safe, but putting a new key or removing one is structural; the removal goes through removeIf and new keys go into a separate map first.
A fail-fast iterator copies the collection's modCount when created and throws ConcurrentModificationException from next() once a structural change has moved it.
basis: section:6.5.3.1. Iteration and Modification in Non-Concurrent Collections

aspects.says: Elements are removed during iteration with removeIf or the iterator's remove, never with the collection's remove inside a for-each loop or a forward index loop.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Removing the second-to-last element of an ArrayList inside a for-each loop throws nothing and silently skips the last element.
A ConcurrentSkipListSet iterator is weakly consistent and keeps sorted order.
basis: section:6.5.3.3. Concurrent Collections and Their Iteration Guarantees
aspects.reason: the sorted skip-list set is practised on page 6.5.1 (ranks); its weakly consistent iteration is the ConcurrentHashMap guarantee this page's quiz asks about

aspects.says: A stream over a non-concurrent collection is subject to the same fail-fast check when its source changes during the pipeline.
aspects.reason: the same modCount check the tracked practice builds, reached through a spliterator; the ledger practice already makes the reader change a map outside its own walk

aspects.says: Only structural changes (adding or removing) trip a fail-fast iterator; setting the value of an existing element or entry does not.
